analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to promptly notify customers of data breaches and provides free credit reports and scores.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House Financial Services subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required banks and other financial institutions to quickly tell customers when a breach exposed their personal information like Social Security or credit card numbers, and to notify credit bureaus and law enforcement. It would have put a fraud alert in affected consumers' credit files so lenders must call the consumer before opening new credit, and it would have given every consumer a free credit report and credit score once a year, plus quarterly free reports for a year after a fraud alert. It also let consumers sue financial institutions that violated the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially identity theft victims. The FTC survey cited in the bill's findings found 27.3 million Americans victimized by identity theft over five years, with $5 billion in out-of-pocket consumer costs. Victims would get automatic fraud alerts, faster notice of breaches, and free access to the credit reports and scores they would otherwise pay for, making it easier to spot and stop fraudulent accounts.

how_it_helps.text: Financial institutions must promptly notify affected customers, the major credit bureaus, and (for large breaches) law enforcement whenever personal information is breached, with FTC-set procedures [S2] [S3].

Credit bureaus must add a fraud alert to a consumer's file when notified by a bank or when the consumer requests one, and must make sure every lender pulling the file knows about the alert and gets the consumer's express authorization before issuing new credit [S2] [S3].

Every consumer gets a free credit report and credit score once each year, and once every three months for a year after a fraud alert is placed; the quarterly cost may be charged to the financial institution that reported the breach, not the consumer [S2] [S3].
Customers injured by a violation can sue for damages, and courts can enjoin violations; these rights stack on top of existing remedies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions bear the cost of monitoring for breaches, notifying customers and bureaus, and potential civil liability. Credit bureaus lose the fees they charged consumers for credit reports and scores that become free, and take on new duties to flag and maintain fraud alerts. Some compliance costs would likely show up as fees passed through to bank customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, other financial institutions, and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The compliance safe harbor is soft: a financial institution is deemed compliant if it follows its own internal security policies, as long as those policies meet the bill's standards, which weakens the guarantee of a standard notice to every affected customer [S3].

Mandatory fraud alerts add friction to legitimate lending: lenders must verify identity and get preauthorization by phone before approving credit for an alerted consumer, which could slow approvals for the consumer and add costs for lenders [S3].
Notification and verification requirements impose real compliance costs on banks and credit bureaus, some portion of which would likely be passed to consumers through fees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the benefits are concrete: earlier warning of breaches, automatic fraud alerts that block new accounts opened in their name, and free visibility into their own credit files. The costs fall mostly on financial institutions and credit bureaus in compliance work and lost fee revenue, and the main design weakness is the self-certification safe harbor that lets a bank substitute its own policies for the standard notice. On balance the bill's protections for victims of a fast-growing crime outweigh its costs, though the safe harbor is a genuine gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2003, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez, a Democrat from Illinois, introduced the bill on October 2, 2003 with no cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].

Three weeks later it was referred to the subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it remained with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote through the end of the 108th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, other financial institutions, and the credit reporting agencies came out ahead: they avoided new breach-notification duties, civil liability, and mandatory free credit reports and scores for the remainder of that Congress.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 2, 2003 and never reported the bill to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 22, 2003 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan split either way.

industries.note: They would have had to place and maintain fraud alerts, warn every lender pulling a file, and provide free credit reports and credit scores they previously charged consumers for. Their lost fee revenue was consumers' savings.

They bear breach-detection, notification, and liability costs, but the FTC survey in the bill's findings put business losses to identity theft at nearly $48 billion in one year, which faster notification and fraud alerts would help curb. Some costs would likely pass to customers as fees.

industries.industry: Companies handling data for financial institutions
industries.note: Vendors that maintain personal information on a bank's behalf would owe prompt breach notification to the institution, adding compliance duties but also sharing responsibility for protecting customer data.
